implementation_notes_raw:
["We have demonstrated improvement in Emergency Department (ED) metrics over the past year; however, there remains room for further improvement. All change ideas identified in the 2025/26 Quality Improvement (QI) Plan have been implemented. Over this period, we have experienced a significant increase in ED patient volume, particularly among high-acuity patients. HRH has also seen a substantial rise in EMS transfers and continues to receive a higher number of ambulances compared to other GTA hospitals, with more CTAS 1–2 patients being transferred. Even with this increased demand, we have achieved measurable improvements in ED performance. We will continue to work collaboratively with the ED and HRH teams to achieve target performance, with a focused emphasis on PIA, EMS offload times, and inpatient bed turnaround time. Notably, for the third consecutive year, we are ranked the #1 Emergency Department in the province based on P4R performance.

Impact of the Change Ideas:
The change ideas had a clear positive impact, helping streamline workflows, improve patient flow, and maintain performance despite rising demand. For example, targeted interventions in PIA and EMS offload contributed to reducing delays and supporting better overall ED efficiency.

Over the past year, we experienced a significant increase in ED patient volume, particularly among high-acuity patients (CTAS 1–2), as well as an increase in EMS transfers compared to other GTA hospitals. Despite these pressures, we successfully implemented all change ideas outlined in the 2025/26 QI Plan and were able to demonstrate measurable improvement in key ED metrics, including PIA, EMS offload times, and inpatient bed turnaround time."]
progress_comments_raw:
["Key Learnings:
1. Collaboration across the ED, HRH, and operational teams is critical to sustaining improvements, especially during periods of high patient volume.
2. Early identification of bottlenecks, such as EMS offload and inpatient bed flow, allows targeted interventions that can have significant impact.
3. Leadership is essential to achieving improvement; guiding teams, fostering engagement, and supporting change makes a measurable difference.
4. When implementing change ideas, it is important to remain open-minded and continuously monitor results. Improvement in one metric may necessitate workflow adjustments elsewhere to ensure balanced performance across the system.
5. Even when patient acuity and volume increase, structured QI initiatives can still drive meaningful improvements if change ideas are fully implemented and monitored.

Advice to Others:
• Fully implement and monitor all change ideas; partial implementation limits impact.
• Engage front-line staff early and maintain ongoing communication to ensure buy-in and sustainability.
• Track key metrics regularly to identify trends, celebrate improvements, and quickly address emerging challenges.
• Recognize that even during periods of high acuity and volume, structured QI approaches can yield measurable gains.
• Strong leadership is key—leaders must guide, motivate, and support teams to achieve meaningful improvement.
• Be open-minded and continuously reassess workflows; improvements in one area may require adjustments elsewhere to maintain overall system efficiency."]

implementation_notes_raw:
["Over the course of Q1 and Q2 we conducted a root cause analysis to identify underlying causes for frequent repeat SPEP, lipid and TSH testing. In terms of reasons for success - 
1) Utilizing Power BI Data - Based on our Power BI dashboard, we were able to readily identify provider groups who were most frequently ordering our laboratory tests of interest within the minimum retesting interval. Having this data readily availlable and stratified by clinical provider group helped us to identify key physician stakeholders who we were able to interview to gauge their insights and perspectives on the underlying root causes of repeat testing, as well as for identifying site specific criteria for appropriateness. 
2) Early and Continuous Engagement with Stakeholders - Our clinician stakeholders were experts from diverse clinical areas including Oncology, Endocrinology, Hematology, Critical Care, Nephrology, Cardiology, Stroke Neurology as well a Registered Dietician. In reflecting on our meetings with our stakeholders, we feel that key elements to successful stakeholder engagement for our team were early involvement, shared goals, as well as regular engagement and integration of stakeholder feedback into our ultimate proposal on site specific repeat testing criteria, and our intervention proposal.  
Challenges - Challenges that we identified throughout our root cause analysis and intervention design included the identification of certain provider groups and clinical scenarios where more frequent repeat testing (prior to our minimum retesting criteria) are appropriate and viewed as critical to facilitating patient care. As such we did receive some pushback with regards to a universal "hard stop" intervention. An additional challenge relates to our laboratory system that would not allow us to exclude certain clinicians/entire provider groups by specialty from our hard stop intervention. As such, we found we were able to most successfully navigate these challenges by both 1) modifying our minimum retesting intervals slightly to ensure we would not be impeding the provision of patient care, and 2) create new laboratory order labels (EX: creating a new lipid panel order only for triglycerides and cholesterol that our Sunnybrook oncologists require in order to monitor patients on immunotherapy more frequently. Details around our site specific recommendations for repeat laboratory testing intervals pertaining to SPEP, TSH and lipid panels can be found in the attached word document with this submission."]

implementation_notes_raw:
["*Flow Coordinator Role Pilot: The pilot successfully trained Flow Coordinators to support offloading by moving “Fit to Sit” and EMS-offloaded patients from the waiting room to the Orange Zone for timely assessment. While the role improved situational awareness and provided staff support, evaluation did not demonstrate meaningful improvement in PIA or overall wait times. Staff and physician feedback rated the role as moderately effective, and benchmarking with peer organizations supported ending the pilot. This reinforced the importance of ongoing evaluation and readiness to pivot when outcomes are not achieved. The team is now exploring alternative flow interventions, including a renewed focus on the Orange Zone Lead role.
*Results of Process Measures:
1. Percentage of Ambulatory EMS Patients who Met the "Fit to Sit" Criteria and Were Placed in the Waiting Area Space, then Moved to the Orange Zone for Assessment: Quantitative data could not be meaningfully extracted for this process measure. When expanded across all ED zones for FY24/25, the median Transfer of Care (TOC) was 0 minutes, defined as the time a patient leaves the “EMS” location code and enters the next location. As a result, TOC time is effectively identical to the next zone “time in” for the majority of cases, with only minor variation where TOC times were manually corrected in NACRS. This limits the usefulness of the metric for performance assessment. Qualitative assessment indicates improvement from Q2 to Q3, reflecting increased proficiency of Flow Coordinators following training, particularly in expediting the movement of “Fit to Sit” and EMS-offloaded patients from the waiting area space to the Orange Zone.
2. Average Number of Patients Waiting to be Seen at Each Hour in the Orange Zone: Remained Consistent Between Q2 (6 Patients, 26.1% of Average Total Patients Waiting to be Seen at Each Hour in the ED) and Q3 (6 Patients, 27.3% of Average Total Patients Waiting to be Seen at Each Hour in the ED). Establishing a fixed target for the "Average Number of Patients Waiting to Be Seen at Each Hour in the Orange Zone" is challenging due to current operational realities. The Diagnostic and Flow Coordinator Role pilot concluded on January 18, 2026 and no longer supports zone-specific flow targets. The primary goal in the Orange Zone is to maintain flow by ensuring the number of patients WTBS exceeds the number of available providers, rather than achieving a specific hourly volume. Additionally, physicians prioritize patients with the longest waits across the department—not solely within the Orange Zone—and patient volumes and acuity vary by time of day, limiting the usefulness of a static hourly target.
3. Completion of Recruitment for Flow Coordinator Role Pilot: Met Target."]

An additional challenge relates to our laboratory system that would not allow us to excude certain clinicians/entire provider groups by specialty from our hard stop intervention. implementation_notes_raw:
["Over the course of Q1 and Q2 we conducted a root cause analysis to identify underlying causes for frequent repeat SPEP, lipid and TSH testing. In terms of reasons for success - 
1) Utilizing Power BI Data - Based on our Power BI dashboard, we were able to readily identify provider groups who were most frequently ordering our laboratory tests of interest within the minimum retesting interval. Having this data readily availlable and stratified by clinical provider group helped us to identify key physician stakeholders who we were able to interview to gauge their insights and perspectives on the underlying root causes of repeat testing, as well as for identifying site specific criteria for appropriateness. 
2) Early and Continuous Engagement with Stakeholders - Our clinician stakeholders were experts from diverse clinical areas including Oncology, Endocrinology, Hematology, Critical Care, Nephrology, Cardiology, Stroke Neurology as well a Registered Dietician. In reflecting on our meetings with our stakeholders, we feel that key elements to successful stakeholder engagement for our team were early involvement, shared goals, as well as regular engagement and integration of stakeholder feedback into our ultimate proposal on site specific repeat testing criteria, and our intervention proposal.  
Challenges - Challenges that we identified throughout our root cause analysis and intervention design inclulded the identification of certain provider groups and clinical scenarios where more frequent repeat testing (prior to our minimum retesting criteria) are appropriate and viewed as critical to facilitating patient care. As such we did receive some pushback with regards to a universal "hard stop" intervention. An additional challenge relates to our laboratory system that would not allow us to excude certain clinicians/entire provider groups by specialty from our hard stop intervention. As such, we found we were able to most succesfully navigate these challenges by both 1) modifying our minimum retesting intervals slightly to ensure we would not be impeding the provision of patient care, and 2) create new laboratory order labels (EX: creating a new lipid panel order only for triglycerides and cholesterol that our Sunnybrook oncologists require in order to monitor patients on immunotherapy more frequently. Details around our site specific recommendations for repeat laboratory testing intervals pertaining to SPEP, TSH and lipid panels can be found in the attached word document with this submission."]

["*Additional Permanent Night Shift Implementation - COMPLETE: The pilot was completed successfully, supported by the implementation of the “Live Wait Time by Zone” dashboard and the new “All Zones” EDIS dropdown, which improved physician visibility of longest waits across care areas. While situational awareness improved, early learning confirmed that data tools alone are insufficient to drive sustained behaviour change. Ongoing work is focused on incremental dashboard enhancements and de-zoning strategies to better align physician practice with patients experiencing the longest waits.
*Physician Prioritization Model Pilot - COMPLETE: The median "PIA Time" target was set at 3 hours: October 2025 exceeded the target, November 2025 was the first month it was achieved, and December 2025 exceeded it again. Monitoring night-shift impacts and incorporating qualitative staff feedback informed flexible, demand-based scheduling decisions. However, reduced physician hours and reliance on time-limited philanthropic funding for the overnight shift present sustainability risks. A key lesson is the need to balance short-term performance gains with long-term funding and workforce stability.
*Flow Coordinator Role Pilot: The Flow Coordinator pilot was completed but did not demonstrate meaningful improvement in PIA or overall wait times. Staff and physician feedback rated the role as moderately effective, and benchmarking with peer organizations supported ending the pilot. This reinforced the importance of ongoing evaluation and readiness to pivot when outcomes are not achieved. The team is now exploring alternative flow interventions, including a renewed focus on the Orange Zone Lead role.
*Triage Workflow Assessment: The PA-at-Triage pilot demonstrated early improvements in PIA, ED LOS, and patient experience; however, staffing turnover created coverage gaps. Based on learnings and peer experience, a short NP-at-Triage PDSA cycle will launch next, followed by a refined PA-at-Triage re-test. Key learnings highlight the importance of provider experience, training, leveraging peer hospitals to replicate successful processes, and phased testing to ensure sustainability and minimize operational risk.

implementation_notes_raw:
["We implemented the standardized post event debrief process on January 31, 2026. Because the process is newly introduced, formal measurement has not yet begun. Prior to implementation, we identified significant inconsistencies in how teams conducted debriefs following incidents—specifically, variation between “hot wash” (immediate) and “cold wash” (later reflection) approaches. The new toolkit now provides a standardized process ensuring that:

• A hot wash debrief occurs immediately following an incident, and
• A cold wash debrief follows to further explore learning opportunities.

Since initiating the new RCA process, we reviewed all corrective actions (CATPR – Corrective Action to Prevent Recurrence). Across all RCAs completed to date, there were a total of 27 CATPRs, of which 4 were determined not feasible as they involved EMR changes that could not be implemented. Of the remaining feasible CATPRs, 11 out of 23 (48%) were completed within 90 days.

Although this represents progress, we remain below the current target of 90% completion within 90 days, as several CATPRs are still in progress. We have identified that this target may need adjustment in the future to differentiate between individual-level corrective actions, which can often be implemented quickly, and system-level corrective actions, such as EMR or organizational process changes, which typically require longer timelines.

To support consistent reporting, we will continue to engage operational teams to ensure all units receive feedback within 90 days of their incident reviews, fostering transparency and continuous improvement. Ongoing data collection will help track implementation timelines and evaluate both the timeliness and effectiveness of corrective actions over time."]

implementation_notes_raw:
["Throughout the year the QIP working group undertook and explored and implemented many change ideas, including the following:
1. Patient Partnership Lead completed phone survey and paper survey of recent discharges to gain input on information provided at discharge and any opportunities for improvement over approximately 2-week period. Results were very positive and provided minimal insights to create additional change ideas. 
2. Introduction of volunteer program to meet with new admissions twice weekly, to explain the Patient Experience Survey, gain consent for electronic distribution and collection of email address. 
3. Explored additional information provision as part of After Visit Summary (AVS). 
4. Exploration of adjusting the expressed consent requirement to implied consent to reduce barriers to survey distribution; environmental scan completed; direction from legal/risk to proceed with moving to implied consent with hopes to increase response rates; work to commence in May once Dovetale upgrade implemented. 
5. Introduction of QR codes to After Visit Summaries to increase survey completion on December 2, 2025. QR codes bypass need for expressed consent. 

Additionally, new information relevant to the adoption of the survey and challenges were realized throughout the year, including:
1. Completing a deep dive on the question asked on the survey. Question is not as simple as “did you receive enough information at discharge” full question is Did you receive enough information from hospital staff about what to do if you were worried about your condition or treatment after you left the hospital?; concerns were raised around framing of question impacting the response. Consultation with Ontario Hospital Association occurred to understand development process of question (and larger survey); inability to reframe question if we wish to continue to peer benchmark. 
2. Peer Benchmarking became available in Q2; Peer benchmarking is still considered exploratory and provisional; peer benchmarking focused on Top 2 box (response of completely and usually) not Top Box which was unknown when establishing QIP.  
 Based on Top 2 Box, the two clinical units perform well on Information at discharge question averaging 89% on 6GI and 91% for 3OBs between April 2025- February 2026. This information would have adjusted the proposed QIP from top box to top 2 boxes.
3. Additionally, due to some updates within Qualtrics and working through unforeseen impacts to SJHH, SJHH survey distribution was paused between September 29 and December 12, 2025. Survey has resumed, and a bolus of survey distribution occurred on December 14, 2025, for patients who met criteria during the pause to distribution. 
 Since resuming survey distribution response rates are lower. Survey responses have dropped from 1563 last year to 1036 this year for the units within the QIP."]

["L’analyse de corrélation menée cette année a permis d’identifier les éléments du sondage ayant le plus d’impact sur la perception des patients en matière de communication. Les résultats de cet exercice ont été partagés avec les parties concernées afin d’informer les actions à venir. 

 

Il ressort de cette analyse que, de façon générale, l’expérience des patients à l’égard du respect et de la courtoisie demeure positive. Cependant, un constat important émerge : plusieurs patients mentionnent ne pas recevoir suffisamment d’information pendant leur séjour. Les questions liées à cet aspect affichent une forte corrélation avec l’expérience globale de communication, ce qui met en lumière l’importance de la transmission claire et complète des renseignements aux patients. 

 

Face à ce constat, une démarche de sensibilisation a été entreprise auprès du personnel. L’accent a été mis sur la nécessité de valider la compréhension des patients, notamment par l’utilisation de questions ouvertes. Cette démarche visait à aligner le contenu des formations avec les besoins exprimés par les différentes parties prenantes. 

 

À la suite de cette analyse, le comité a décidé de déployer une nouvelle formation Osoin  qui s'harmonise avec la manière renouvelée de se présenter et d'interagir avec les patients et les partenaires de l'organisation. Cette approche met l'accent sur la sensibilité à l'équité, à la diversité et à l'inclusion, favorisant ainsi une offre active des services en anglais et en français, un environnement accueillant et respectueux pour tous. 

 

La formation s'appuie sur divers scénarios illustrant le quotidien de plusieurs groupes au sein de l'organisation. Elle est accessible via une plateforme en ligne, ce qui permet d'assurer un suivi rigoureux des participants et de garantir la conformité des audits."]

progress_comments_raw:
["Partially implemented as intended – full roll out April 2025 

Full Lessons Learned: 

Timely notification of bed availability and TOA completion remains a challenge due to reliance on MPV color changes without automated alerts. Inconsistent staff monitoring of MPV results in missed notifications and unexpected patient arrivals. Stronger accountability is needed to ensure bed status updates and TOA completion before transfers. 

The transition from MPV to Meditech adds complexity, requiring dual-system usage as Meditech’s housekeeping module and messaging functionality remain underdeveloped. This limits automated communication and prolongs reliance on MPV. 

Inconsistent adherence to TOA protocols has led to staff dissatisfaction, union concerns, and patient handoff issues. Addressing these concerns requires improved training, clearer expectations, and system enhancements. 

Potential Solutions & Next Steps: 

Explore activating Meditech’s messaging system for automated bed status notifications. 

Develop an ED-facing dashboard to display bed status and prompt timely TOA completion. 

Maintain verbal TOA as an optional but available clarification tool. 

Implement regular audits and real-time feedback to improve compliance. 

Investigate communication tools (Hypercare, Teams, Meditech messaging) for TOA efficiency. 

Strengthen leadership accountability measures to address non-compliance."]

planned_methods_raw: ["• Validate and review data. • Create internal workflows to capture this data daily. • Develop an internal structure to review patients waiting greater than 2 hours. • Add this indicator to ED Quality Committee and Inpatient/Medicine scorecards for monitoring and discussion of QI initiatives. • Understand impacts for patients requiring isolation on IPU and delays related to accommodating in appropriate space on IPU. • Involve IPAC • Ensure patients are not admitted before they are ready for transfer from ED to IPU. • Consider developing exclusion criteria within the new hospitalist model."]
process_measures_raw: ["Number of admitted patients waiting in ED spaces at 0800: Tracking the number of patients waiting in both conventional and unconventional ED spaces for a bed in the hospital."]
process_targets_raw: ["Number of admitted patients waiting in ED spaces: By the end of Q4 the number of admitted patients waited in conventional and unconventional emergency department spaces for a bed in the hospital (include all service or bed types) does not significantly increase."]
implementation_notes_raw:
["ARH continues to monitor the number of admitted patients remaining in ED spaces at 0800. Performance this year is 0.15, slightly above last year’s 0.14, this has been reported as a 7.14% decline. Based on operational review, this change is likely related to patients with high acuity or complexity being admitted but remaining in the ED until clinically stable enough for the inpatient unit (IPU). This practice has contributed to higher counts of admitted patients occupying ED spaces at the morning reporting time.

Successes
- Improved understanding of patient flow issues: Case reviews helped clarify that increases in the 0800 metric relate more to patient acuity and appropriateness for the IPU than to bed availability alone.

- Progress toward policy standardization: Work is well underway on a policy to guide physicians in determining which patients are appropriate for admission to the IPU versus those who must remain in the ED until stable. This includes safe handover practices and clarity around MRP at specific times of day. 

- Strengthened cross‑department collaboration: Multiple committees and clinical stakeholders have contributed to policy development, improving alignment across the organization.

Challenges
- Premature admissions to IPU: Some patients who are not yet clinically appropriate for the IPU are being admitted, increasing the count of admitted patients remaining in ED spaces at 0800. 

- High-acuity patient volumes: Higher acuity levels in the ED mean more patients require extended stabilization in the ED before transfer to an inpatient bed.

- Ongoing practice variability: Despite progress, there is still inconsistency in how physicians determine readiness for transfer to the IPU.

Results, Barriers, and Enablers
Results: The number of admitted patients in ED spaces at 0800 increased minimally from 0.14 to 0.15. While not a significant operational change, it exceeds the target of maintaining or improving performance.

Barriers: Lack of a standardized policy guiding physician decision‑making for IPU appropriateness.
High acuity setting placing pressure on ED space and workflow.

Enablers: Active policy development with broad stakeholder engagement. Increased awareness among physicians and leaders regarding the impact of early admission decisions. Improved communication between ED and inpatient teams."]
progress_comments_raw: ["Although ARH reported a slight decline in performance for admitted patients in ED spaces at 0800, this trend is closely linked to patient acuity and challenges determining IPU readiness rather than a deterioration of patient flow. With a new policy nearing completion, increased cross‑team collaboration, and growing awareness of appropriate admission criteria, ARH is positioned to stabilize and improve performance in the coming fiscal year."]

implementation_notes_raw:
["ARH continued its work this fiscal year to improve the accuracy and reliability of PIA data for CTAS 1 and 2 patients, with a focus on reviewing high‑acuity cases and identifying EMR workflows that better capture physician initial assessment times. Although progress was made in establishing review processes and standardizing workflows, ARH did not meet the target, with current performance at 4.9 hours compared to the provincial target of 4.0 and 4.67 last year.

Successes

- Regular review of high‑acuity cases: ARH increased oversight of CTAS 1 and 2 charts, particularly where PIA exceeded one hour. These reviews created a clearer understanding of workflow delays and documentation gaps.

- Improved collaboration with ED physicians: Engaging physicians in discussions about PIA performance helped identify peak volume times and potential opportunities to improve coverage and flow.

-EMR workflow exploration: Preliminary work was completed to map current documentation practices and assess where additional Meditech workflows could support more accurate capture of PIA times. In addition conversations have begun related to how PIA will be captured in future state EPIC (Oct 2026) 

Challenges

- Worsening PIA performance: Higher patient acuity and increased ED volumes compared to our regional peers and compared to previous years contributed to longer PIA times and added pressure on physician resources.

- Data accuracy issues: Similar to ambulance offload reporting, PIA data often did not reflect real clinical activity. Physicians frequently did not use the Meditech functions designed to record PIA, leading to under‑captured or inaccurate timestamps.

- Incomplete adoption of EMR workflows: Identifying additional EMR solutions proved difficult within the current system capabilities in addition to navigating resistance to change within the ED MD group. 

Process Measures: Results, Barriers, and Enablers

Results: Reviews of high‑acuity cases improved understanding of workflow challenges, though the goal of reviewing 100% of CTAS 1 and 2 cases with PIA > 1 hour by Q4 was not consistently met due to competing operational priorities. EMR workflow improvements were assessed but not fully implemented.

Barriers: Rising acuity and volume, inconsistent physician use of Meditech PIA functions, limitations within the current EMR, and operational pressures impacting timely documentation. Lack of a Business Intelligence tool at ARH means that all extraction and validation are done manually, requiring significant staff time and slowing improvement efforts

Enablers: Engagement of ED physicians in data review, strengthened collaboration across the P4R working group in particular Health Records, growing awareness of documentation expectations, and improved analytics capacity to support case review."]
progress_comments_raw: ["Although PIA performance did not meet targets this year, ARH strengthened its understanding of documentation challenges, gained clearer insight into physician coverage needs, and laid groundwork for EMR and workflow improvements leading into the implementation of EPIC. These steps position the organization for more targeted progress in the next fiscal year."]

Successes

-Foundational structures built: Biweekly and weekly audit processes were developed, providing the basis for more reliable monitoring.

implementation_notes_raw:
["Triage Reassessment Nurse Role 
  The implementation of the Triage Reassessment Nurse role has contributed to a reduction in patients leaving without being seen (LWBS) by ensuring regular reassessment, timely escalation of care, and improved monitoring of patients waiting for physician assessment. 

Virtual Home Waiting Room 
  The ED Virtual Home Waiting Room has demonstrated positive impact with reductions in time to Physician Initial Assessment (PIA), LWBS rates, and overall Emergency Department length of stay. In addition, patient feedback indicates improved satisfaction related to reduced waiting room congestion and the ability to wait at home. 

Flow Nurse Role, Chair Care Model, and Additional Waiting Areas 
  The combination of the Flow Nurse role, expanded hallway recliner chair capacity, and additional internal waiting spaces has improved patient flow throughout the department. These initiatives have supported more efficient use of treatment rooms and contributed to reductions in overall length of stay (LOS). 

Staff Engagement and Adoption of New Initiatives 
  Successful engagement of nursing and physician staff has supported the implementation of multiple new roles and processes. Front‑line involvement and acceptance of these changes have been key to embedding improvements into daily operations and sustaining progress toward improved PIA performance. 

Challenges 

Inpatient Overcapacity Impacting ED Flow 
  Ongoing overcapacity in inpatient units has limited the availability of inpatient beds, contributing to congestion within the Emergency Department and delays in patient movement. This has had downstream impacts on treatment room availability and time to Physician Initial Assessment (PIA). To mitigate this, a new organizational surge plan has been implemented to support earlier escalation and improved coordination across programs. As this surge plan is relatively new, there continue to be implementation and workflow adjustment challenges as teams adapt to new processes. 

Physician Coverage and Staffing Constraints 
  Consistent physician coverage remains a challenge due to a provincial reduction of physician hours by approximately 11 hours per day, compounded by ongoing physician recruitment challenges. Reduced physician availability can impact the sustainability of early‑assessment improvements and timely PIA performance, particularly during peak volumes and surge periods. 

Mitigation Strategies for Medical Staffing Challenges 
  To help offset physician staffing constraints, the ED has implemented mitigation strategies including the utilization of Nurse Practitioners (NPs) and Physician Assistants (PAs), in addition to ongoing process improvements. While these strategies have supported care delivery and patient flow, physician coverage remains a key risk to sustaining PIA performance improvements."]

implementation_notes_raw:
["A number of key lessons learned emerged from this year's Discharge Communication QIP, including:

1. Value of the Teach Back Method: Consistent use of the Teach Back method has been identified as an important skill in enhancing patient and family/caregiver discharge communication. The Teach Back method helps staff understand how to communicate information meaningfully by having patients/caregivers repeat education back, in their own words. This also provides in-the-moment feedback to staff on opportunities to revise their approach and strengthen subsequent teaching. Patient and staff feedback indicate that broader use of this method can improve comprehension and confidence.

2. Consistent Use of Patient Whiteboards: Patient and caregiver feedback emphasized how important patient whiteboards are as a communication tool. For example, our whiteboards can help to identify who a patient wants involved in their care; enhance communication between patient/family/caregivers and care team; and provide valuable and accessible key updates at-a-glance. Continued focus is needed to support reliable, organization-wide adoption of whiteboard practices to ensure patients receive these important updates more consistently.

3. Identifying and leveraging Family/Caregiver "Key Moments": Work with frontline teams identified many "Key Moments" when engaging family/caregivers may have the greatest impact. These insights helped determine department-specific and organization-wide opportunities for enhancing family/caregiver involvement; however, momentum on this decreased over the course of the year to focus on other priorities for this QIP driver. Sustained and renewed attention may help to maximize the benefits of these insights.

4. Balancing Competing Priorities During Quality Improvement Work: Teams initially planned regular QIP-related discussions during departmental quality improvement huddles, though operational demands at times reduced the frequency and depth of these conversations over the course of the year. This affected frontline engagement and overall progress on implementation of change ideas. progress_comments_raw: ["Time to Inpatient Bed improved by 13.6 hours year over year, driven by coordinated, multipronged efforts across the organization.  For our 2026/27 Quality Improvement Plan, we have chosen indicators that directly support our refreshed organizational strategy and goals. Capacity continues to be Trillium Health Partners’ greatest constraint. Improving capacity and flow remains one of our top priorities for the year ahead, driven through reducing hospitalization initiatives that will ease capacity pressures, enhance patient and caregiver experience, strengthen team experience, support financial sustainability, and enable us to deliver equitable, high-quality care for the health of our community. Challenges 
Patient flow continues to be significantly impacted by high medicine bed demand, with the medicine census remaining elevated, often requiring patients to be admitted to alternate units. In response to system pressures, the Ontario Health directive to flex up to 120% occupancy in acute care beds has been activated. However, late discharges and delays in discharge planning are contributing to bottlenecks in bed availability. Additionally, Short Stay Treatment Unit (SSTU) beds are currently staffed using Emergency Department resources, which may further strain ED capacity.
